    A Family businesses face several challenges and opportunities in the UAE, such as:

The overlap of these roles tends to create tensions and conflicts that increase as the number of family members increases. These conflicts can have detrimental effects on the business.

    Frequently Asked Questions

    These are some of the most frequently asked questions:

    1. What are the main sources of criminal law in the UAE?

    The main sources of criminal law in the UAE are the Federal Penal Code, the Federal Criminal Procedure Code, and the laws and decrees issued and regulated by the federal and local authorities. The Federal Penal Code defines the general principles of criminal liability, the types and degrees of punishments, and the rules for applying them. The Federal Criminal Procedure Code regulates the procedures for investigation, prosecution, trial, and appeal of criminal cases. The laws and decrees issued by the federal and local authorities supplement or amend the provisions of the Federal Penal Code and the Federal Criminal Procedure Code on specific matters.

    2. What are some of the major differences between the criminal law system in the UAE and other countries?

    One of the major differences between the criminal law system in the UAE and other countries is that the UAE follows a civil law system, which means that the judges rely on written laws and codes rather than on precedents or case law. Another difference is that the UAE applies Islamic law (Sharia) in certain areas of criminal law. Such as adultery, apostasy, theft, and alcohol consumption. Sharia law prescribes specific punishments for these offenses, such as flogging, stoning, amputation, or death. However, these punishments are rarely applied in practice and are subject to judicial discretion and review.

    3. What are some of the common crimes and penalties in the UAE?

    Some of the common crimes and penalties in the UAE are:

    • Theft: punishable by imprisonment for up to three years or a fine.
    • Fraud: punishable by imprisonment for up to two years or a fine.
    • Forgery: punishable by imprisonment for up to five years or a fine.
    • Assault: punishable by imprisonment for up to one year or a fine.
    • Murder: punishable by death or life imprisonment.
    • Drug trafficking: punishable by death or life imprisonment.
    • Drug possession: punishable by imprisonment for up to four years or a fine.
    • Alcohol consumption: punishable by imprisonment for up to six months or a fine.

    4: What are some of the legal rights and obligations of a person accused of a crime in the UAE?

    Some of the legal rights and obligations of a person accused of a crime in the UAE are:

    • The right to remain silent and not to incriminate oneself.
    • The right to be informed of the charges and evidence against oneself.
    • The right to have legal representation and access to a translator.
    • The right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty.
    • The right to a fair and public trial before an independent and impartial court.
    • The right to appeal against the verdict and sentence.
    • The obligation to cooperate with the authorities and comply with their orders.
    • The obligation to respect the laws and customs of the UAE.

    These are some of the most frequently asked questions:

    1. What are the main sources of criminal law in the UAE?

    The main sources of criminal law in the UAE are the Federal Penal Code, the Federal Criminal Procedure Code, and the laws and decrees issued and regulated by the federal and local authorities. The Federal Penal Code defines the general principles of criminal liability, the types and degrees of punishments, and the rules for applying them. The Federal Criminal Procedure Code regulates the procedures for investigation, prosecution, trial, and appeal of criminal cases. The laws and decrees issued by the federal and local authorities supplement or amend the provisions of the Federal Penal Code and the Federal Criminal Procedure Code on specific matters.

    2. What are some of the major differences between the criminal law system in the UAE and other countries?

    One of the major differences between the criminal law system in the UAE and other countries is that the UAE follows a civil law system, which means that the judges rely on written laws and codes rather than on precedents or case law. Another difference is that the UAE applies Islamic law (Sharia) in certain areas of criminal law. Such as adultery, apostasy, theft, and alcohol consumption. Sharia law prescribes specific punishments for these offenses, such as flogging, stoning, amputation, or death. However, these punishments are rarely applied in practice and are subject to judicial discretion and review.

    • Assault: punishable by imprisonment for up to one year or a fine.

    • Drug trafficking: punishable by death or life imprisonment.
    • Drug possession: punishable by imprisonment for up to four years or a fine.
    • Alcohol consumption: punishable by imprisonment for up to six months or a fine.

    Some of the legal rights and obligations of a person accused of a crime in the UAE are:

    • The right to remain silent and not to incriminate oneself.
    • The right to be informed of the charges and evidence against oneself.
    • The right to have legal representation and access to a translator.
    • The right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty.
    • The right to a fair and public trial before an independent and impartial court.
    • The right to appeal against the verdict and sentence.
    • The obligation to cooperate with the authorities and comply with their orders.
    • The obligation to respect the laws and customs of the UAE.

    2. What are the benefits of registering under the new law?

    The Law is based on a voluntary registration system, which means that family businesses can choose whether to register under the Law or not. However, registering under the Law may provide some benefits and incentives for family businesses, such as:

    • The ability to create different classes of shares with different rights and obligations, which is a ground-breaking development for onshore limited liability companies (LLCs).
    • The possibility of obtaining special benefits and incentives from the federal and emirate level authorities, such as tax exemptions, subsidies, preferential treatment in government contracts, etc.
    • The access to bespoke dispute resolution processes specific for family businesses, such as arbitration, mediation and conciliation.
    • The support from accredited advisers and corporate service providers who can assist family businesses with their legal, financial and administrative matters.

    3. How can family businesses register under the new law?

    Family businesses can register under the Law by entering into a family ownership contract, which is a written agreement among the family members who own the majority of the shares or assets of the family business. The family ownership contract should include:

    • The identification of the family members who are parties to the contract and their respective shares or assets.
    • The objectives, vision and mission of the family business.
    • The governance structure and rules of the family business, such as the board of directors, management team, committees, etc.
    • The succession plan and procedures for transferring shares or assets among family members or to third parties.
    • The dispute resolution mechanisms for resolving any conflicts among family members or with third parties.

    The family ownership contract should be registered with the competent authority in each emirate where the family business operates. The registration fees and procedures may vary depending on the emirate.

    4. What are some of the best practices for family businesses under the new law?

    Family businesses should follow some best practices to ensure their sustainability and competitiveness under the new law, such as:

    • Adopting a clear and transparent governance structure that defines the roles and responsibilities of each family member and ensures accountability and oversight.
    • Developing a comprehensive succession plan that ensures a smooth transition of leadership and ownership from one generation to the next.
    • Seeking professional advice from accredited advisers who can help with legal, financial and administrative matters related to the family business.
    • Following the principles of proper governance and good conduct that are prescribed by certification and accreditation programs under the new law.

    2. What are the types of due diligence audit?

    There are different types of due diligence audit, depending on the scope and purpose of the transaction. Some of the most common types are:

    • Financial due diligence: This involves reviewing the target company's financial statements, working capital, cash flow, assets, liabilities, and tax compliance. It aims to verify the accuracy and reliability of the financial information provided by the target company.
    • Legal due diligence: This involves reviewing the target company's contracts, agreements, licenses, permits, litigation, intellectual property rights, and regulatory compliance. It aims to identify any legal risks or issues that may affect the transaction or the future operations of the target company.
    • Operational due diligence: This involves reviewing the target company's business processes, systems, policies, procedures, human resources, customers, suppliers, and competitors. It aims to assess the efficiency and effectiveness of the target company's operations and its competitive position in the market.

    3. How long does a due diligence audit take?

    The duration of a due diligence audit depends on several factors, such as the size and complexity of the target company, the availability and quality of information, the level of cooperation from the target company's management and staff, and the scope and depth of the audit. Generally speaking, a due diligence audit can take anywhere from a few weeks to several months to complete.

    4. How much does a due diligence audit cost?

    The cost of a due diligence audit varies depending on the type and extent of the audit, as well as the experience and reputation of the auditor. The cost may also depend on whether the auditor charges a fixed fee or an hourly rate. Typically, a due diligence audit can cost from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of Dirhams.

    A financial statements audit is the appraisal of a company’s financial statement by an independent auditor.     2. Why is a financial statements audit important?

    A financial statements audit is important for several reasons. First, it provides assurance to the shareholders, investors, creditors, regulators, and other stakeholders that the company’s financial performance and position are reliable and transparent. Second, it helps the company to identify and address any errors, frauds, risks, or weaknesses in its financial reporting system. Third, it enhances the company’s reputation and credibility in the market.

    3. Who can perform a financial statements audit in the UAE?

    Only licensed auditors who are registered with the Ministry of Economy and the relevant authorities can perform a financial statements audit in the UAE. The auditors must follow the International Standards on Auditing (ISA) and the UAE Federal Law No. 2 of 2015 on Commercial Companies.

    4. Is a financial statements audit mandatory for all companies in the UAE?

    A financial statements audit is mandatory for all companies in the mainland and some parts of the free zones in the UAE. The companies must appoint an auditor within four months of their incorporation and submit their audited financial statements to the authorities within four months of their fiscal year-end.

Free zone entities are registered in one of the many free zones in the UAE, which offer tax exemptions, 100% foreign ownership and other incentives, but they can only operate within their respective free zone or outside the UAE.     The UAE offers a number of advantages for doing business, such as:

    • A strategic location between Asia, Europe and Africa, with access to a large and diverse market of over two billion people.

    The UAE also poses some challenges for doing business, such as:

    • A complex and dynamic legal system, with different laws and regulations applicable in different emirates, free zones and offshore jurisdictions.
    • A high cost of living and doing business, with expensive rents, utilities, labor and transportation.
    • A competitive and saturated market, with many local and international players vying for customers and opportunities.
    • A cultural and linguistic diversity, with different customs, norms and expectations among different nationalities and communities.
